en: *The Record of the Eminent Monk Faxian*, one fascicle.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of the Eastern Jin Dynasty concerning his travels in India.
Formerly, while in Chang’an, Faxian lamented that the Vinaya-piṭaka was incomplete; thereupon, during the Hongshi era...
In the second year, when the year was Jihai (479 CE),
he entered into a covenant with Huijing, Daozheng, Huiying, Huiwei,
and others to travel together to India in search of the Vinaya.
Setting out from Chang’an,
he crossed the Long Mountains and reached the kingdom of Qiannui, where he observed the summer retreat.
Upon concluding the summer retreat, he proceeded to the kingdom of Rutan.
He traveled from Mount Duyang to the town of Zhangye.
Because Zhangye was in great turmoil and the roads were impassable,
the King of Zhangye treated him with great hospitality and retained him as his patron (dānapati).
Thereupon, he met with Zhiyan, Huijian, Sengshao, Baoyun, Sengjing, and others;
rejoicing in their shared aspirations,
they sat together in summer retreat.
Having completed the summer retreat, he proceeded further to Dunhuang.
There was a pass extending eighty *li* from east to west and forty *li* from north to south.
They stayed together for over a month.
Faxian and four others set out ahead with the envoys,
while they parted from Baoyun and the rest at Dunhuang.
The Prefectural Governor Li Hao provided him with provisions for crossing the Shahe River.
Within the Shahe River there were many malevolent spirits and scorching winds;
those who encountered them all died, and not a single person survived.
Above there were no flying birds, and below there were no running beasts.
Gazing as far as the eye could reach in every direction, one sought a place to cross but knew not where to direct one's steps;
there were only the bleached bones of the dead to serve as markers.
Traveling for seventeen days, covering approximately fifteen hundred *li*,
one can reach the kingdom of Shanshan.
Its terrain is rugged and its soil is thin and infertile.
The clothing of the laypeople is roughly the same as that of the land of Han,
differing only in their use of felt and coarse woolen cloth.
Their king reveres the Dharma.
There are more than four thousand monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
The laypeople and śramaṇas of various countries all practice the Dharma of India;
there are only differences in their degree of refinement or coarseness.
From here, all the countries traversed traveling westward were of this same character;
the only difference was that the local languages varied from country to country.
Nevertheless, those who had left the household life in each place studied the scripts and languages of India.
He stayed there for one month. Then,
traveling northwest for fifteen days, he reached the country of Wuyi,
where there were also more than four thousand monks.
All were students of the Hīnayāna,
and their discipline was uniform and orderly.
When śramaṇas from the land of Qin arrived there, they were not included among the ranks of the monastic community at all.
Faxian obtained a tally for official travel from Gongsun Jingli.
He stayed for more than two months,
after which he returned and joined with Baoyun and others at the state of Wuyi.
The people there did not cultivate rites and ceremonies and were extremely inhospitable to guests.
Thus, Zhìyán, Huìjiǎn, and Huìwéi turned back toward Gāochāng in search of travel provisions.
Fǎxiàn and the others, however, received supplies from Lord Fú and Gōngsūn.
He was thus able to proceed directly toward the southwest;
along the way, there were no inhabited settlements,
and his journey was fraught with hardship.
The suffering he endured was beyond comparison with anything in human experience.
After traveling for one month, on the fifth day of the month, he arrived at Khotan.
That country is prosperous and joyful, and its population is vast and flourishing.
All of them reverently uphold the Dharma and delight one another with the joy of the Dharma.
The assembly of monks numbers tens of thousands.
Those who study the Mahāyāna all receive communal meals;
the people of that country dwell in star-like clusters.
Small stupas were erected before every household door;
the smallest of these were approximately twenty feet high.
Monastic quarters for the community of monks were constructed to provide for visiting monks.
Furthermore, the king provided for the needs of Faxian and his companions by settling them in a monastery.
The name of this monastery was Gomatī;
it was a Mahāyāna temple.
Three thousand monks ate together at the signal of the *gandī* drum.
When they entered the refectory, their deportment was uniform and solemn as they sat down in order;
all was silent, and not a sound arose from their bowls or dishes.
The attendants (karmadāna) were not permitted to call out to one another while serving food;
they were to signal only by pointing their fingers.
Huijing, Daozheng, and Huida set out first toward the country of Kacha.
Faxian and his companions wished to witness the procession of the sacred image and stayed for three months.
In that country, there were four great monasteries (*saṃghārāma*), not counting the smaller ones.
From the first day of the fourth month, the city streets were swept and sprinkled, and the lanes were adorned.
Great canopies were spread over the city gates,
and everything was magnificently decorated.
The king, his consort, and their court ladies all reside therein.
Gomatīsaṃgha is a follower of the Mahāyāna and is held in high esteem by the king.
First, regarding the procession of the image:
twenty-four *li* outside the city, they constructed a four-wheeled image carriage over three *zhang* in height.
It was shaped like a traveling palace,
adorned with the seven treasures,
and hung with silken banners and canopies.
The image stands within a chariot, attended by two bodhisattvas who act as celestial attendants;
all are adorned with gold and silver carvings and suspended in mid-air. The image is situated one hundred paces from the gate.
The King removed his celestial crown, changed into new robes, and went barefoot,
holding flowers and incense, escorted by his attendants, out of the city. He welcomed the image,
prostrating himself with his head at its feet, scattering flowers and burning incense.
As he entered the city,
ladies and court ladies atop the gate towers scattered various flowers from afar, which fell down in profusion.
Such were the ornaments and offerings, each chariot being uniquely adorned.
In each monastery, the image procession takes place for one day;
beginning on the first day of the month,
it continues until the fourteenth day when the procession is concluded.
When the procession of the image was completed, the king and his consort returned to the palace.
Seven or eight *li* to the west of the city is a monastery named the King’s New Monastery (*Rājanavasaṃghārāma*).
Its construction began eighty years ago and was only completed during the reigns of three successive kings.
It stands twenty-five zhang high;
its surface is carved and engraved with intricate patterns, covered in gold and silver, and composed of a multitude of precious gems.
Behind the stupa, a Buddha hall was constructed, exquisitely adorned;
its beams, pillars, doors, panels, windows, and lattices were all covered with gold leaf.
Separate monastic quarters were also built, likewise magnificent and elegantly decorated.
It cannot be fully described in words.
The kings of the six kingdoms to the east of the ridge possess many precious objects of the highest value, most of which they offer as religious offerings;
those used by people for personal purposes are few.
After the four months had passed and the image procession was completed,
Sengshao went alone with a Hu monk toward Jibin,
while Faxian and the others proceeded toward the kingdom of Subhūti.
After traveling for twenty-five days on the road,
he arrived at that kingdom.
The king was diligent in his practice, and there were more than a thousand monks.
Having studied the Mahāyāna for a long time and stayed here for fifteen days,
he then traveled south for four days and reached the Pamir Mountains.
He arrived at Huiguo (Huiguó) for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Having completed the retreat, he traveled twenty-five days by mountain path to reach Jiesha (Qiéchā) country,
where he rejoined Huijing and the others.
It happened that the king of that country was holding a pañcavārṣika festival.
"Pañcavārṣika" means, in the language of Han, a great quinquennial assembly.
At the time of the assembly, he invited śramaṇas from the four directions.
They all came and gathered like clouds.
Having assembled, they adorned the seating places for the saṃgha,
hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies.
Having fashioned golden and silver lotus flowers, they were placed behind the monks' seats;
pure sitting mats were spread out,
and the king and his ministers made offerings according to the Dharma.
It may last for one month, two months,
or three months;
it most often occurs during the spring season.
After the King had held the assembly, he further exhorted his various ministers to provide offerings and perform acts of veneration for one day,
two days, three days, five days, or even up to seven days.
When the offerings were fully completed, [he departed].
The king provided his own horse, complete with saddle and bridle, for the noble ministers of the kingdom to ride;
he also gave him many white cotton cloths and various kinds of precious treasures, as well as all items required by a śramaṇa.
Together with his ministers, he made a vow to offer the land as a gift to the Sangha;
having offered it to the Sangha, he subsequently redeemed the land from them.
Because the mountain was cold, no other grains grew there.
It was merely ripe barley.
Once the community of monks had completed their annual retreat (varṣā), frost would invariably fall that very morning;
therefore, the king would regularly invite the monks so that the barley would ripen.
Thereafter, they performed the ceremony of receiving the year's alms.
Within that country was a Buddha’s spittoon,
which was made of stone.
The color [of the relic] resembles that of a Buddha’s almsbowl.
There is also one tooth of the Buddha;
the people of that country have erected a stupa for this Buddha-tooth.
There were more than a thousand monks,
all of whom studied the Hīnayāna.
From this mountain eastward, the clothing of the laypeople was for the most part similar to that of the land of Qin.
They also differ in their use of felt and coarse woolen cloth;
the religious practices of these śramaṇas are even more excellent and cannot be recorded in full.
That country lies in the midst of the Pamir Mountains.
From the Pamir Mountains onward, the vegetation, fruits, and grains are all different;
only three things—the bamboo, the pomegranate, and the sugarcane—are the same as those in the land of Han.
From here, traveling westward, one reaches the kingdom of Northern India.
After traveling for one month on the road, he crossed the Pamir Mountains.
On these mountains, there is snow both in winter and summer,
and there are also venomous dragons.
If its intent is thwarted, it will unleash poisonous winds,
snow, rain, and flying sand and gravel;
those who encounter such calamities will not one in ten thousand survive.
The people of that land call it the Snow Mountains (Himavat).
Having crossed the ridges, he arrived in Northern India and first entered its territory.
There was a small kingdom named Tālikā,
where there were also many monks who all studied the Hīnayāna.
In that country, there had formerly lived an arhat.
Using his supernormal power,
he took a skilled craftsman up to Tuṣita Heaven to observe the height, proportions, and physical appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva;
having returned, he carved a wooden image.
After three successive upward contemplations from front to back,
the image was finally completed.
It was eight *zhang* tall, with a foot and pedestal measuring eight *chi*.
On days of fasting, there is always radiance;
the kings of various nations vied with one another to offer worship.
He now remains present here for that reason.
Traveling southwest along the ridge for fifteen days,
the path was arduous and the cliffs and banks were precipitous and impassable;
the mountains there consisted solely of stone walls rising sheer to a height of a thousand fathoms.
Facing it, his eyes grew dizzy;
wishing to advance, he cast himself forward,
yet his feet found no place to set down.
There is a river named the Sindhu.
In ancient times, people excavated a path through the rocks and provided side ladders; there were seven hundred in total.
Having crossed the ladder, he stepped onto a suspended rope to traverse the river.
The distance between the two banks of the river was less than eighty paces,
as recorded by the nine successive translators.
Zhang Qian and Gan Ying of the Han dynasty both did not reach this far.
The monks asked Faxian:
"Can the beginning of the Buddha-dharma's eastward transmission be known?"
Xian said,
"I inquired of the local people of that land,
and they all said:"
According to ancient tradition,
after a statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva was established,
there subsequently arrived a śramaṇa from India.
Those who carried the Sūtras and Vinaya across this river [established] images approximately three hundred years after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa;
calculating by the era of King Ping of the Zhou dynasty, [this corresponds to that period].
From this it may be seen that the proclamation and dissemination of the Great Teaching began with this image;
were it not for the Bodhisattva Maitreya following in the footsteps of Śākyamuni, [this would not have been possible].
Who could have caused the Three Jewels to be proclaimed and spread so that people on the frontiers would recognize the Dharma?
One surely knows that the opening of this mysterious destiny was fundamentally not a matter of human effort;
thus, the dream of Emperor Ming of the Han had its underlying cause.
Having crossed the river, he arrived at the kingdom of Udyāna.
This kingdom of Udyāna is located directly to the north of Central India (Madhyadeśa).
All its inhabitants speak the language of Central India.
Madhyadeśa, known as the Middle Kingdom,
has customs regarding clothing and food that are identical to those of China.
The Buddha-dharma flourishes there greatly.
A place where the community of monks resides is called a saṃghārāma.
There are five hundred such saṃghārāmas in total,
all of which follow the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
If any visiting bhikṣus arrive, they shall all be provided for for three days.
Once the three days have passed, they are then instructed to seek their own lodgings.
This has been the constant tradition.
When the Buddha reached Northern India,
he arrived at this very country.
The Buddha left his footprints here.
Whether long or short, it depends on the thoughts within the human mind;
even to this day, it remains so.
Furthermore, the stone for drying robes and the place where the evil dragon was subdued are both still present today.
The stone is fourteen feet high and approximately twenty feet wide;
one side is flat.
Huijing, Huida, and Daozheng—these three set out first toward the country of Nagarahāra, where the Buddha’s shadow is located.
Faxian and his companions remained in this country for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
When the retreat was concluded, they traveled south to the country of Śūhṛta.
The Buddha-dharma was also flourishing in that country.
It was here, in the place where the celestial Śakra, in a former life, tested the Bodhisattva by transforming himself into a hawk and a dove so that he might cut his own flesh to ransom the dove,
that the Buddha, having already attained enlightenment, traveled together with his disciples.
It was said,
"This is the very place where I originally cut my own flesh to ransom the dove. From this,
the people of the country came to know [the truth].
A stūpa has been erected at this site, adorned with gold and silver.
From here, traveling eastward for five days, one arrives at the kingdom of Gandhāra.
This was the domain ruled by Dharmavivardhana, the son of King Aśoka.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva,
he also gave his eyes to others in this country;
at that site, a great stūpa was likewise erected, adorned with gold and silver.
The people of this country mostly study the Hīnayāna.
Traveling east from here for seven days,
there is a country named Takṣaśilā.
Cakravāḍaśīrṣa (竺剎尸羅) means "cutting off the head.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva,
he gave his head to others at this very spot.
For this reason, they were named accordingly.
Traveling eastward again for two days, one arrives at the place where [the Bodhisattva] threw himself to feed a starving tigress;
at these two locations, great stūpas were also erected.
All were adorned with various precious jewels;
kings, ministers, and commoners vied with one another to offer worship,
scattering flowers and lighting lamps in an unending succession.
Including the two aforementioned stupas, the people of that region also refer to them as the Four Great Stupas.
Traveling four days south from the kingdom of Gandhāra, one arrives at the kingdom of Peshawar (Puruṣapura).
In the past, when the Buddha was traveling through this country with his disciples,
he said to Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a king named Kaniṣka."
A stūpa was erected at this site.
Later, when King Kaniska appeared in the world and went forth on a tour of inspection, he arrived there.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to awaken his mind,
transformed himself into a young cowherd boy and erected a stūpa by the side of the road.
The king asked,
"What have you done? He replied:
"Build a stūpa for the Buddha.
The king said, "Excellent!
Thereupon, the king immediately erected a stūpa upon the small child's stūpa.
It is over forty zhang in height and adorned with various precious jewels.
Among all the stupas and temples he has ever seen or passed by, none can compare to its magnificence and solemnity.
Tradition says:
Among all the stupas in Jambudvīpa, this stupa alone is the most supreme.
Once the King had completed the construction of the stupa, a small stupa spontaneously emerged beside it to the south of the great stupa,
reaching a height of about three feet.
The Buddha’s almsbowl is currently located in this country.
In the past, the King of the Yuezhi raised a great army and came to attack this country,
desiring to take the Buddha’s almsbowl.
Once this country had been subdued,
the King of the Yuezhi and his followers, being deeply devoted to the Buddha-dharma,
wished to take the alms bowl with them as they departed.
Therefore, he made grand offerings.
Having completed his worship of the Triple Gem,
he adorned a great elephant and placed the bowl upon its back.
The elephant then prostrated itself on the ground and was unable to move forward.
He then had a four-wheeled carriage made to carry the bowl;
even when eight elephants pulled it together, they still could not advance.
The King, knowing that the conditions for the bowl’s arrival had not yet matured,
felt deep remorse and sighed; he immediately erected a stūpa and a saṃghārāma at this very spot,
and left various offerings there to guard it.
There were more than seven hundred monks.
When the sun was about to reach its zenith, the assembly of monks would bring forth their alms bowls,
and laypeople would provide various kinds of offerings.
Thereafter, one partakes of the midday meal.
At evening, when it is time to burn incense, it is done again in the same manner.
It can hold approximately two *dou*.
It is multicolored with black predominating, its four borders clearly defined;
it is two inches thick and possesses a brilliant luster.
When a poor person throws a few flowers into it, it becomes full immediately.
There was a man of great wealth who wished to make offerings with many flowers;
even a hundred thousand million *hu* would never have sufficed.
Baoyun and Sengjing, however, simply made offerings to the Buddha’s bowl and then returned.
Huijing, Huida, and Daozheng first headed toward the country of Nagarahāra to pay homage to the Buddha’s shadow,
his tooth relic, and his cranial bone.
Huijing fell ill, so Daozheng remained there to attend to him.
Huida alone returned to the kingdom of Puruṣapura, where they met [the others].
Huida, Baoyun, and Sengjing then returned to the land of Qin;
Sengjing passed away at the Buddha Bowl Monastery.
Thereupon, Faxian proceeded alone toward the site of the Buddha’s cranial bone.
Traveling sixteen yojanas to the west, he reached the city of Hilo on the border of the kingdom of Nagarahāra.
Within that city was a vihāra containing the Buddha’s cranial bone.
It was entirely adorned with gold leaf and the seven precious gems.
The king held the skull bone in such high esteem that he feared others might plunder it.
He then selected eight men of prominent lineage from within the kingdom;
each man held one seal,
which was used to seal and guard [the relics].
At dawn, the eight persons arrive together and each examines their seal.
Thereafter, they open the door.
Having opened the door, they wash their hands with fragrant water.
He brought forth the Buddha’s cranial bone and placed it upon a high pedestal outside the vihāra;
it was set upon a round anvil made of the seven precious gems, beneath which was a bell of lapis lazuli, all adorned with pearls and jewels.
The bone is yellowish-white in color,
four inches square,
and its surface is elevated.
Every day after [the sun] has risen, the people of the monastery ascend a high tower to beat a great drum, blow a conch shell, and strike a bronze bowl.
Upon hearing this, the King proceeds to the monastery to make offerings of flowers and incense.
Having made the offerings, he received them upon his head in succession and departed.
Entering through the eastern gate, he exited through the western gate.
Thus did the king perform offerings and prostrations every morning.
Only then did he attend to the affairs of state.
Householders and elders likewise first made offerings before attending to their own household affairs;
they did so day after day, never once growing weary or indolent.
When the offerings were all completed, he returned the cranial bone to the vihāra.
There was a stūpa of liberation made of the seven precious gems,
which would sometimes open and sometimes close.
It is about five feet high and used for holding [offerings]. Every morning,
there are always people selling flowers and incense in front of the gate of the vihāra.
Those who wished to make offerings would purchase [the site] with various means,
and kings also constantly sent envoys to provide offerings.
Although the surrounding area was thirty paces square, even when heaven shook and the earth split apart, this place remained unmoved.
Traveling one *yojana* north from here, one arrives at the city of the kingdom of Nādikā.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva, in a former life, purchased five stalks of flowers with silver coins to make an offering to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Within the city there is also a stūpa for the Buddha’s tooth,
which is venerated according to the rites for the cranial bone.
One yojana to the northeast of the city, [is...]
Arriving at the mouth of a valley, he found a Buddha’s mendicant staff (*khakkhara*).
He also constructed a vihāra there as an offering;
the staff was made of gośīrṣa sandalwood.
It was approximately six or seven zhang in length;
when placed inside a wooden cylinder,
even a hundred thousand people could not move it.
Entering the valley mouth and traveling west, there was a Buddha’s *saṃghāṭī* robe;
he also constructed a vihāra to make offerings to it.
At that time, the local customs of that country were suffering from a severe drought.
At that time, the people of the country led one another out with their robes to pay homage and make offerings.
Immediately, the heavens sent down a great rain.
To the south of the city of Rājagṛha, at a distance of half a yojana, there was a stone chamber on a broad mountain.
To the southwest is where the Buddha left his shadow;
standing about ten paces away from here, it appears like the true form of the Buddha,
with its golden complexion, marks of excellence, and radiant brilliance clearly manifest.
As one draws closer, it becomes increasingly subtle and faint, appearing as if it were there;
though the skilled painters sent by the kings of various directions attempted to copy it, none could succeed.
Thus the people of that country have handed down the tradition.
All the thousand Buddhas shall leave their shadows here.
Approximately four hundred paces to the west of the shadow is where the Buddha shaved his hair and clipped his nails during his lifetime.
The Buddha himself, together with his disciples,
constructed a stūpa seven or eight zhang high as a model for the future practice of stūpa construction;
it remains there even today.
On the outskirts is a monastery containing more than seven hundred monks.
In this place, there are thousands of stupas for various arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
They stayed here for three months of winter.
Faxian and two others then crossed the Lesser Snow Mountains to the south.
In these Snow Mountains, snow accumulates both in winter and summer.
In the northern shade of the mountain, a violent cold wind suddenly arose, causing everyone to shiver with cold.
Huìjǐng alone could no longer endure it and pressed forward;
foam issued from his mouth as he spoke to Fǎxiǎn, saying: [He passed away.]
"I shall not return to life either.
You should depart at once; do not die together with me.
Thereupon, he passed away.
Faxian stroked it and wailed in grief:
"My original plan has not been fulfilled; what can be done about fate?
He then exerted himself once more, managed to cross the ridge, and arrived south of the pass in the country of Lāḍha.
Recently, about three thousand monks, studying both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
have resided here for the summer retreat;
having completed their retreat, they will travel south.
After traveling for ten days, they arrived at the country of Bāṇa,
where there were also about three thousand monks,
all of whom studied the Hīnayāna.
From here, traveling east for three days, one again crosses the Sindhu River.
Both banks are level plains.
Beyond the river lies a country named Vida.
The Buddha-dharma flourished there, encompassing both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna studies.
Upon seeing that a Daoist from the Qin had come,
he felt great compassion and spoke these words:
How is it that people in the borderlands can recognize those who have left home to practice the Way, seek out the Buddha-dharma from afar,
provide them with all their necessities,
and treat them according to the Dharma?
From here, traveling southeast for less than eighty *yojana*s,
one passes through many monasteries with tens of thousands of monks;
having traversed these various places, one arrives at a certain kingdom.
The kingdom is named Mathurā.
Furthermore, one passes by the Pūrṇa River,
on both banks of which there are twenty saṃghārāmas.
There were approximately three thousand monks,
and the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly.
This was true for all the various kingdoms of India to the west of the River Sha (the Taklamakan Desert).
The king was deeply devoted to the Buddha-dharma and made offerings to the assembly of monks.
On such occasions, he would remove his celestial crown and,
together with his kinsmen and ministers, personally serve the food with his own hands.
After the food distribution was completed,
he spread a mat upon the ground and sat before the elder (upādhyāya) at the head of the assembly of monks,
not daring to sit upon a bed.
The ritual protocols for the royal offerings made to the Buddha during his lifetime have been transmitted down to the present day.
From this point southward, the region is known as the Middle Kingdom (Madhyadeśa).
In China, the cold and heat are harmoniously balanced, and there is no frost or snow.
The people are prosperous and happy, and there are no household registers or official laws.
Only those who cultivate the King’s lands pay a share of the produce.
He departs when he wishes to depart and stays when he wishes to stay.
The king’s governance does not employ execution;
those who commit offenses are merely fined money.
According to the gravity of the offense,
even if one plots an evil rebellion,
it shall not exceed the amputation of the right hand.
The king’s attendants and those on his left and right all receive stipends.
All the people of the kingdom refrain from killing living beings;
they do not drink alcohol and do not eat onions or garlic.
The only exception is the caṇḍāla;
the caṇḍāla is called an evil person and dwells separately from others.
If they enter a city or town, they strike a wooden block to distinguish themselves;
people then recognize them and avoid them so as not to brush against them.
Within the country, they do not raise pigs or chickens, nor do they sell living beings.
In the cities there are no butcher shops or taverns.
For trade, cowrie shells are used;
only the caṇḍālas and fishermen sell meat.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various kings, elders,
and lay devotees erected monasteries for the Saṃgha, providing them with fields,
houses, gardens, orchards, households, oxen, and calves, all recorded in formal iron-bound deeds.
Subsequently, from king to king, they transmitted this practice through generations, none daring to abolish it;
thus it continues uninterrupted to this day.
The monastic community resides in these dwellings.
Their bedding, food and drink, and clothing were entirely free from deficiency;
this was the case everywhere.
The community of monks constantly took the performance of meritorious deeds as their primary occupation.
Furthermore, when reciting sutras or practicing seated meditation,
visiting monks arrive and the resident monks go out to welcome them,
carry their robes and bowls for them, and provide water for washing their feet.
Having been provided with oil for his feet and non-timely medicinal gruel,
and having rested for a short while, he was again asked about his seniority in the monastic order;
subsequently, he was assigned a room and bedding.
In various ways according to the Dharma,
stupas for Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda, as well as stupas for the Abhidharma, the Vinaya, and the Sūtras, were erected at the monastic residences.
One month after the summer retreat, families seeking merit were exhorted to provide offerings.
The monks partook of non-timely beverages.
The great assembly of the Sangha gathered for a Dharma discourse.
Having finished the discourse, they made offerings at the stupa of Śāriputra.
